question_html: Under Section 2(20) of the Companies Act, 2013, a company means-

options.A: a company incorporated under this Act or under any previous company law
options.B: any association of persons formed for the acquisition of gain, whether registered or not
options.C: any body corporate incorporated outside India having a place of business in India
options.D: a partnership firm registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932

answer_html:
Answer: (A) a company incorporated under this Act or under any previous company law.

In terms of the Companies Act, 2013, company means a company incorporated under the Act or under the previous company law [Section 2(20)]. A company is an artificial, legal and juristic person, separate from its members and having perpetual existence.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The principle that a company is a distinct legal person existing independently of its members is best illustrated by the decision of the House of Lords in-

options.A: Bacha F. Guzdar v. C.I.T.
options.B: Salomon v. Salomon & Co.
options.C: Royal British Bank v. Turquand
options.D: Foss v. Harbottle

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Salomon v. Salomon & Co..

[(1898) AC 22]. Option (C) is the authority for the doctrine of indoor management and option (A) for the proposition that shareholders are not the owners of the company's property.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Perpetual succession means that-

options.A: the liability of the members continues even after they cease to be members
options.B: the membership of a company may keep changing from time to time, but that does not affect the company's continuity
options.C: the company must be re-registered every time a member dies or becomes insolvent
options.D: the shares of the company are freely transferable in the open market

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the membership of a company may keep changing from time to time, but that does not affect the company's continuity.

Perpetual succession means that the membership of a company may keep changing from time to time, but that does not affect the company's continuity. The death or insolvency of individual members does not in any way affect the corporate existence of the company - members may come and go but the company can go on forever.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Which of the following is a recognised circumstance in which the courts will lift the corporate veil?

options.A: In every case where the company has made a loss for three consecutive years
options.B: Whenever the company has more than one class of shareholders
options.C: Where there is avoidance of welfare legislation, or where fraud or improper conduct has been committed
options.D: Whenever a shareholder requests the court to examine the company's internal affairs

answer_html:
Answer: (C) Where there is avoidance of welfare legislation, or where fraud or improper conduct has been committed.

The corporate veil is lifted, among other situations, in the law relating to trading with the enemy, in matters of taxes and duties where controlling interest is in issue, where subsidiaries act as agents, where welfare legislation is being avoided, where fraud or improper conduct is committed, where the corporate personality is abused for an unjust purpose and to protect public policy.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under Section 2(68) of the Companies Act, 2013, the articles of a private company must limit the number of its members to-

options.A: one hundred, except in the case of a small company
options.B: seven, except in the case of a One Person Company
options.C: two hundred, except in the case of a One Person Company
options.D: fifty, in every case without exception

answer_html:
Answer: (C) two hundred, except in the case of a One Person Company.

A private company is one which, by its articles, restricts the right to transfer its shares, limits the number of its members to two hundred except in the case of a One Person Company, and prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe for any securities. Persons in the employment of the company and former employees who continue as members are excluded from the count, and joint holders are treated as a single member.

question_html: Under Section 2(6), significant influence for the purpose of determining whether a company is an associate company means control of at least-

options.A: twenty per cent of total share capital, or of business decisions under an agreement
options.B: fifty-one per cent of the paid-up share capital, or of business decisions under an agreement
options.C: more than one-half of the total voting power, whether exercised on its own or with its subsidiaries
options.D: ten per cent of the issued share capital, or of the composition of the Board of Directors

answer_html:
Answer: (A) twenty per cent of total share capital, or of business decisions under an agreement.

An associate company, in relation to another company, means a company in which that other company has a significant influence but which is not a subsidiary of the company having such influence, and includes a joint venture company. Significant influence means control of at least twenty per cent of total share capital, or of business decisions under an agreement. question_html: Under Section 464 read with Rule 10 of the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014, no association or partnership formed for the acquisition of gain may consist of more than-

options.A: 20 persons in the case of a banking business and 10 in any other case
options.B: 100 persons, unless the Central Government grants an exemption
options.C: 200 persons, unless it is a Hindu undivided family
options.D: 50 persons, unless it is registered as a company or is formed under any other law in force

answer_html:
Answer: (D) 50 persons, unless it is registered as a company or is formed under any other law in force.

No association or partnership consisting of more than 50 persons as per Rule 10 shall be formed for the purpose of carrying on any business having for its object the acquisition of gain, unless it is registered as a company under the Act or formed under any other law in force. The provision does not apply to a Hindu undivided family carrying on business, or to an association or partnership formed by professionals governed by special Acts. Every member of such an illegal association is punishable with a fine up to one lakh rupees and is personally liable for all liabilities incurred.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: A company has paid-up share capital of ₹50 crore, free reserves of ₹30 crore and a securities premium account of ₹10 crore. Without prior approval by a special resolution, the aggregate of its loans, guarantees, security and acquisitions of securities may not exceed-

options.A: ₹48 crore
options.B: ₹54 crore
options.C: ₹40 crore
options.D: ₹90 crore

answer_html:
Answer: (B) ₹54 crore.

The ceiling is 60% of paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium account, or 100% of free reserves and securities premium account, whichever is more. Here 60% of (₹50 + ₹30 + ₹10) crore = ₹54 crore and 100% of (₹30 + ₹10) crore = ₹40 crore. The higher figure, ₹54 crore, is the limit. Option (C) takes the lower of the two tests and option (A) applies 60% to free reserves plus paid-up capital only.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under Section 123(1), no dividend shall be declared or paid by a company for any financial year except out of-

options.A: the securities premium account of the company, to the extent it has not been applied for any other purpose permitted by the Act
options.B: the amount standing to the credit of the capital redemption reserve, after providing for depreciation for the year in question
options.C: the profits of the company for that year after providing for depreciation, or the undistributed profits of previous years after providing for depreciation, or out of both
options.D: any reserve of the company, whether free or otherwise, provided the Board considers that reserve adequate for the purpose

answer_html:
Answer: (C) the profits of the company for that year after providing for depreciation, or the undistributed profits of previous years after providing for depreciation, or out of both.

question_html: In computing the profits out of which dividend may be declared, which of the following must be excluded?

options.B: Any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets, and any change in the carrying amount of an asset or liability on measurement at fair value

question_html: The rule in Foss v. Harbottle is that-

options.A: the majority shareholders owe a fiduciary duty to the minority in every transaction
options.B: no action can be brought by a member in respect of a wrong alleged to be done to the company, the company itself being the proper plaintiff

answer_html:
Answer: (B) no action can be brought by a member in respect of a wrong alleged to be done to the company, the company itself being the proper plaintiff.

Foss v. Harbottle, 67 E.R. 189, (1843) 2 Hare 461 lays down the principle of non-interference by the court with the internal management of a company: no action can be brought by a member against the directors in respect of a wrong alleged to have been committed to the company, and the company itself is the proper party. case_facts_html:
Godavari Alloys Limited is a company having a share capital. Its register of members shows 900 members and its issued share capital is ₹50 crore.

A group of 80 members, who between them hold shares of ₹6 crore nominal value and who have paid all calls and other sums due on their shares, believe that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to their interests. They wish to apply to the National Company Law Tribunal for relief.

They are advised that Section 244 lays down alternative eligibility tests, and that where an applicant does not meet them the Tribunal has a power that may still assist.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. If the group had held shares of only ₹4 crore nominal value, its correct course would be to-

options.A: apply to the Central Government for an exemption from Section 244
options.B: requisition an extraordinary general meeting and pass a special resolution authorising the application
options.C: abandon the application, since the Act provides no relief in such a case
options.D: apply to the Tribunal to waive all or any of the requirements of Section 244 so as to enable it to apply under Section 241

answer_html:
Answer: (D) apply to the Tribunal to waive all or any of the requirements of Section 244 so as to enable it to apply under Section 241.

Shares of ₹4 crore would be below the one-tenth threshold of ₹5 crore, and 80 members would remain below the 90-member threshold, so neither alternative test would be satisfied. The proviso to Section 244 nevertheless empowers the Tribunal, on an application made to it in that behalf, to waive all or any of the requirements so as to enable the members to apply under Section 241.
